extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military officers, military lawyers, convening authorities
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and established rules governing the conduct, powers, limits, and duties of courts-martial, judge advocates, counsel, court members, and accused persons in military trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel/advisor presence and testimony order
rubrics_metrics.description: A party (e.g., civil counsel assisting the judge advocate) may be permitted by the court to remain in the courtroom and advise with the judge advocate during the trial; in some cases he has been allowed to be accompanied by his own counsel. If such a party is to testify, he should ordinarily be the first witness examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may permit presence at discretion; when such a party will testify, ordinarily examine first (not invariable). See R. 2,1, June 1863; 29,34, June 1869.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge advocate entitled to closing argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge advocate in our practice is entitled to the closing argument or address to the court, and he may present an address although the accused waives his right to present any; the function of the judge advocate at this stage of the proceedings not being confined merely to replying to the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court is not authorized to deny the judge advocate this right. However, the judge advocate is not authorized to read to the court evidence or written statements not introduced upon the trial and which the accused has had no opportunity to controvert or comment upon. (R. 11, 377; R. 22, 238.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to transmit completed record
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the court was convened by a military officer it is the duty of the judge advocate, upon the completion of the record, to transmit the same to such officer (or his successor in command) for the proper action; where convened by the President, to transmit the completed proceedings directly to the Judge Advocate General in order that he may exercise revisory functions reposed in him by section 1199, R. S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmission duties arise from statute and practice; see R. 42, 457, Dec. 1879 and Army Regulations (paragraphs cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge advocate challengeability
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge advocate is not subject to challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a general rule (R. 35, 618, Oct. 1874). Under custom the judge advocate may also challenge for cause in some circumstances (C. 2059, Feb. 1896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's discretion to try by court-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Except by the authority of express statute, an accused can never be entitled to be tried by court-martial; where he is amenable to trial, the Government may cause him to be tried or may waive a trial, at discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: R. 34, 413, Aug. 1873; P. 65, 259, June 1894. Emphasizes prosecutorial/convening authority discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Amendment principle in courts-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution, but not the amendment itself, applies to courts-martial trials as a part of our common law military; an accused on trial before a court-martial cannot, when testifying as a witness in his own behalf, be compelled by it to incriminate himself as to an offense in respect to which he has not testified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies as a common-law principle though statutory provisions may differ (C. 1495, July 1895).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of medical records for identity evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an accused denies that he is the person described in the charges, evidence of identity may be introduced which was secured by surgeons of the Army at the time of the physical examination required by the Regulations and recorded in the regular records, or which was secured when the accused was a patient under such surgeons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible identification evidence from official medical records. (C. 24624, Mar. 13, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No special privileges for high-rank officers on defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the accused is an officer of high rank should not be regarded as constituting a ground for allowing him any special right or privilege in his defense before a court-martial; all persons are equal before the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartial administration required; citation R. 11, 204, Dec. 1864.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on restraining the accused during trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused on trial before a court-martial should be subjected to no restraint other than such as may be necessary to enforce his presence or prevent disorderly conduct; placing irons upon him is not justified except in extreme cases where there is reasonable ground to believe he will attempt to escape or commit violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in extreme cases preferable to place an adequate guard rather than irons. (R. 31, 102; 32, 274, 633.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force by officers not excused except in self-defense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a sufficient defense to a charge of striking or using other violence against a soldier, by an officer, that the soldier was violent and insubordinate, unless it clearly appears that the force employed by the officer was resorted to in self-defense, or that the soldier could not have been repressed by usual legitimate methods of discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force must be clearly necessary and proportionate; citations R. 53, 193; P. 43,52.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation not a defense for insulting/assaultive written communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving insulting or threatening language from another officer does not constitute legal provocation to justify the accused's sending a highly abusive and insulting written communication; proper redress is complaint to a superior and preferring charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course taken by accused (retaliatory writing) is unmilitary and unbecoming; provocation is not a legal defense. (P. 65, 285.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of pay account offense standard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a sufficient defense to a charge of duplication of a pay account that the accused had an understanding with the first assignee to delay presentation; the fact that a second account is presented while the first remains outstanding completes the offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agreement between parties does not excuse the offense of presenting duplicate accounts. (P. 50, 4-5, 219; C. 15373.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on introducing new charges after trial begun
rubrics_metrics.description: After the accused has been arraigned, has pleaded, and the trial has been entered upon, new and additional charges which the accused had no notice to defend cannot be introduced nor the accused required to plead thereto; such charges should be made the subject of a separate trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects right to notice and to exercise challenge; see R. 24, 513 and 577.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of variance objections at arraignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A failure at arraignment to take notice of a variance between the form of a specification and the specification as it appeared in the copy of the charges served at his arrest is a waiver of the objection, and the same cannot be taken advantage of later in the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objection timing is critical; P. 64, 172, Mar. 1894.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intoxication by prescribed drugs may excuse offense if sole cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Drunkenness caused by morphine or other drug prescribed by a medical officer of the Army or civil physician may constitute an excuse for a breach of discipline provided it clearly appears that this was the sole cause of the offense and the accused was not negligent or at fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defence limited to cases where prescribed drug alone caused incapacity; R. 28, 390.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to orders as defense limited when order illegal
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of a commanding officer will generally constitute sufficient authority for acts done by an inferior in compliance; however, if the order is palpably illegal the inferior cannot justify under it, and it will be admissible only in extenuation of the offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subordinate duty of obedience balanced against manifest illegality of orders; see cases cited (Fair, McCall v. McDowell, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for objection to unsigned charge
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection that a charge is not signed should be taken at the arraignment—when the omission may be supplied by the judge advocate's affixing his signature. By pleading the general issue the accused waives the objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise signature defects at arraignment to preserve objection (P. 59, 258).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution may charge alternative forms; no election required
rubrics_metrics.description: The prosecution is at liberty to charge an act under two or more forms where doubtful under which it is more properly brought; in military practice the accused is not entitled to call upon the prosecution to 'elect' under which charge it will proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accused cannot force election; see R. 33, 306.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel presence discretionary but usually conceded
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or soldier put on trial before a court-martial is not entitled as of right to have counsel present with him, but the privilege is one which is almost invariably conceded; where unreasonably refused such refusal may constitute ground for disapproval of proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court not required to delay an unreasonable time to enable accused to provide counsel. (R. 32, 519; R. 30, 102.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-arraignment access to counsel and witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused, prior to arraignment, even if in close arrest, should be allowed interviews with counsel, military or civil, as he may have selected; counsel should be permitted to interview any accessible military person who may be a material witness for the accused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects preparation for defense; R. 12, 31, 21; G. 13892, Dec. 29, 1902.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuitability of certain officers as defense counsel at post
rubrics_metrics.description: No officer directly responsible for the discipline of an organization at his command (commanding officer of a post, band, company, battalion, squadron, regiment) nor the trial officer of a summary court will be regarded as a 'suitable' officer for detailed duty as defense counsel at that post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to prevent conflicts of interest and preserve fairness; per Circular 8, Adjutant General's Office, 1894.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of an officer detailed as counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers detailed as counsel should perform duties which usually devolve upon counsel in civil criminal courts so far as apposite to military procedure, employ all honorable means to acquit the accused and invoke every defense which the law and facts justify, regardless of their own opinion of guilt or innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officer-counsel must advocate vigorously within legal and service customs. (P. 64, 164; various opinions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No government payment for civil counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: All application by an accused officer to be furnished at the expense of the United States with civil counsel to defend him on his trial by court-martial is unprecedented and will not be entertained; no authority exists for payment by the United States of civil counsel employed by an officer or enlisted man to defend him on trial by court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accused must bear costs of private civil counsel. (P. 50, 277; P. 32, 165.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government policy re reimbursement for defense expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the policy of the Government to incur expenses for defending officers before military courts from the consequences of their misconduct, and counsel should look to the accused for reimbursement for any expenses incurred as counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel should seek reimbursement from client in misconduct cases. (G. 13470, Oct. 20, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused's statement/admission not evidence but considered
rubrics_metrics.description: In any case tried by court-martial the accused may present a statement or address either verbal or in writing; such statement is not evidence, but as a personal defense or argument it may and properly should be taken into consideration by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement may influence court but is not formal evidence; R. 20, 432.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of admissions in accused's statement
rubrics_metrics.description: While the statement is not evidence, if the accused clearly and unequivocally admits facts material to the prosecution such admissions may be viewed by the court and reviewing officer as practically facts in the case; a full admission may waive objection to irregularity in proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions in a statement may bind accused for adjudicative purposes. (R. 27, 407; R. 27, 385.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on accused's freedom of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A large freedom of expression in his statement to the court is allowable, especially in comments upon the evidence; an accused may reflect within reasonable limits upon the apparent animus of his accuser, but personal attacks not apposite to the facts or marked disrespect toward the court are not legitimate and may be ordered omitted as a condition to continuing the address or filing it with the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may require omission of improper matter; R. 27, 520.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signed written statements/pleas appended to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the accused submits a written statement or interposes a plea, such plea or statement should be signed by him, or by counsel in his behalf, and appended to the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal signature requirement for records; C. 18764, Nov. 9, 1910.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication after acquittal may be offense
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication by an officer, after his acquittal, of the statement presented by him to the court in which he reflected in violent and vituperative language upon the motive and conduct of an officer of the same regiment, denounced him as devoid of gentlemanly instincts and a disgrace to the service—held to constitute a serious military offense to the prejudice of good order and military discipline, and not excused because the court had permitted the statement to be made and recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-trial publications can create new offenses despite prior allowance in court. (R. 33, 582; 34, 186.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of acquittal
rubrics_metrics.description: An acquittal leaves the accused in the condition in which he was before the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final effect: restoration of prior status; C. 1418, June 6, 1895.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding a court member after material trial parts discouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: To add a new member to a military court after any material part of the trial has been gone through must always be most undesirable and not to be resorted to except in exceptional cases to prevent failure of justice; adding a member after all testimony is introduced and nothing remains except finding and sentence is without precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary remedy only; II. J1, 525, Mar. 1879.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member testifying does not invalidate proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: While it is generally undesirable that a member of a military court should testify as a witness (except perhaps as to character), the fact that he is called to testify does not affect the validity of the proceedings and does not debar him from exercise of his duties or rights as a member including deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Member remains entitled to participate in deliberations, admissibility issues, and votes. (R. 26, 216.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of member: notification and record
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of a court-martial prevented from attending should communicate the cause of his absence to the president or judge advocate so that it may be entered in the proceedings; on reappearing after absence, failure to offer explanation justifies the president asking for a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures record of absences and transparency; R. 30, 315.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer not exempt from arrest due to court membership
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer is not exempt from arrest by virtue of being at the time a member of a general court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrest should, if practicable, be avoided while engaged on court-martial duty but remains possible. (R. 7, 320.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of discharge/resignation on membership
rubrics_metrics.description: If during trial a member is served with a legal order dismissing or discharging him or official notice of acceptance of his resignation, he becomes separated from the Army and can no longer act upon the court and should withdraw, with the order entered on the record; but expiration of term of service pending trial does not necessarily disqualify him until actually discharged or mustered out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different effects depending on formal separation vs. mere term expiration. (R. 11, 203; R. 16, 111.)

rubrics_metrics.name: President of the court by seniority; no special qualifications required
rubrics_metrics.description: No special rank or qualifications are required for the position of president of a military court; the president is simply the senior in rank of the members present and presides by virtue of seniority alone. The senior present at termination authenticates the proceedings as president.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seniority determines presidency; R. 30, 246; C. 5332.

rubrics_metrics.name: President's limited original authority
rubrics_metrics.description: While the president has special authority to swear the judge-advocate (statutory), in other respects he has no original authority but acts as the representative and 'organ' of the court in performing usual presiding duties and authenticating the proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President's role is mainly procedural and representative. (R. 30, 246.)

rubrics_metrics.name: President has no command power over members
rubrics_metrics.description: The president of a military court has no command as such and cannot give orders to any other member; he gives directions necessary for the conduct of proceedings, but failure to comply may constitute conduct prejudicial to good order rather than disobedience of a lawful command of a superior officer under article 21.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: President equals other members in deliberations and votes; no superior command authority. (R. 30, 246, 315.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial powers are statutory and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has only statutory powers and therefore can exercise no common-law functions such as the general power to punish for contempt; their cognizance is confined to classes of offenses recognized by the military code and their function is criminal—awarding punishment for military offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No authority to adjudge damages, rescind contracts, or pass on civil rights; see B. 27, 454; 0. 3608, 11196, 17768.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of authentication of charges transmitted by convening commander
rubrics_metrics.description: To be taken cognizance of by the court it is not essential that a charge should be signed by any officer; if duly officially transmitted by the convening commander or other competent superior authority to the court in terms to try or for action, it is sufficiently authenticated for trial and arraignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transmission by competent authority cures signature absence; R. 55, 369; P. 59, 258.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's limited power to strike/reject charges
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial is not authorized, of its own motion, to reject or strike out a charge or specification formally referred to it for trial, nor to direct the judge advocate to drop or withdraw such charge; authority of the convening commander is requisite, except the court may allow a special plea or objection and quash or strike out the charge when sufficiency of pleading is put in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must refer most charging decisions to convening authority unless plea raises sufficiency; R. 29, 370.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance and quorum rules for members
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where it sustains a challenge under article 88, a court-martial is not authorized to dispense with the attendance of a member; it cannot excuse a member to enable him to attend to other duties (e.g., act as counsel) without relief by the convening authority. If five members remained present during absences of others, validity of findings and sentence not affected absent prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict practice but preserves validity where quorum maintained; multiple citations (P. 15, 48; various G ops.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating of members must follow convening order
rubrics_metrics.description: A general court-martial has no authority to seat members in any order of rank different from that indicated by the convening order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seating must conform to convening order; C. 15262.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court cannot place judge advocate in arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: For the court or the president to place or order the judge advocate in arrest would be an unauthorized proceeding; punishment or arrest of such officer can only be imposed through the convening authority or other competent commander (though contempt proceedings under article 86 may apply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects independence/role of judge advocate; R. 3, 603; 21, 629.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court has no authority to arrest accused or compel attendance by its own order
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has no authority over the person of an accused except when he is before it for trial; it cannot arrest him nor by its own order cause him to be brought to the place of trial—the compelling of his attendance is duty of the convening officer or post commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement of attendance is an executive duty, not judicial. (R. 22, 606; 39, 44.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court cannot assign counsel or compel officers to act as counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: A military court has no authority to assign counsel to an accused unprovided with counsel and has no power to compel an officer to act as counsel for an accused; nor can it excuse one of its members to enable him to act as counsel for an accused except by convening authority relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocation of counsel is outside court power; R. 13, 400; R. 35, 440; P. 57, 417.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may procure attendance of witnesses via judge advocate or convening authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court desires testimony of a party not introduced by prosecution or defense it may properly call upon the judge advocate to have such party summoned, or, if military, apply to convening authority/post commander to have him ordered before it to testify, and it may adjourn for a reasonable time to await attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court has procedural means to obtain witnesses but relies on judge advocate/convening authority; R. 25, 578.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena of telegraph operators and non-privilege of telegrams
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial (by subpoena duces tecum, through the judge advocate) may summon a telegraph operator to appear before it and bring with him a certain telegraphic dispatch; telegrams are not privileged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telegraphic communications may be compelled and used as evidence; P. 31, 149; C. 20085.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court has no authority to arrest witness suspected of false swearing
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has, as such, no authority to arrest, or to require its judge advocate or other officer to arrest, a witness suspected of false swearing upon a trial which has been had before it; its proper course is to report the facts to the convening authority for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perjury/fraud suspected after trial must be reported, not acted on by court arrest. (B. 3, 109.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts-martial jurisdiction limited to military offenses; no civil remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts-martial are bodies of exceptional and restricted powers; their cognizance is confined to distinctive classes of offenses recognized by the military code; their jurisdiction is criminal and they have no authority to adjudge damages for personal injuries or private wrongs, rescind contracts, or pass upon civil rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts convened solely to award punishment for military offenses; (B. 27, 454; 0. 3608; 11196; 17768.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court cannot be used to collect private debts of officers
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial cannot be availed of for the collection of private debts of officers and can take no notice of their financial obligations except as evidence of fraud or dishonor when admissible in proof of an offense under the Articles of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial matters are civil unless relevant as evidence of a military offense. (P. 35, 463.)
